Opening hours

Open when the bread is ready, closed when it is gone. In practice that means early, and in practice it means the last hour of the day is a negotiation.

Shaping in two stages

Shape in two stages with a twenty-minute rest between them. The first gathers the dough into a rough round and the second tightens it. Attempting both at once tears the surface, and a torn surface spreads in the oven however carefully it was proofed. The rest is not optional and it is not idle time: the gluten relaxes enough to be shaped again without fighting back.

Scoring

Score once, deeply, just before the loaf goes in. One confident cut opens better than several shallow ones, and a blade held at an angle produces the ridge people associate with a good bake. None of this changes the taste, which is worth saying plainly: scoring is presentation, and presentation is allowed to be the reason.

Reading the crumb

Large irregular holes mean a wet dough handled gently; an even fine crumb means a stiffer dough or more thorough shaping. Neither is better. A dense band along the bottom means the loaf went in before it was ready, and a collapsed dome means it went in after it was past ready — the two failures look nothing alike and are an hour apart in the same schedule.

Oven spring

Most of the rise happens in the first eight minutes, while the crust is still soft and the water inside is turning to steam. Anything that stiffens the crust early — a dry oven, too low a temperature, an unnecessary early door opening — takes that rise away, and no amount of proofing afterwards puts it back.
